name: DiffEqGPU.jl (GPU ensemble ODE solvers in Julia, GPUTsit5) vs MPGOS
baseline: MPGOS (Massively Parallel GPU ODE Solvers), a CUDA C++ ensemble ODE solver library: RK4 (fixed step) and RKCK45 (adaptive), built with nvcc -O3
workload: Lorenz system (3 states, float32), ensemble of 8 to 8,388,608 parameter sets (R from 0 to 21) integrated over t in [0,1] with dt 0.001 on one GPU; fixed-step and adaptive (Julia reltol=abstol=1e-8) variants; wall time per whole ensemble solve in ms.
claimed_speedup: No speedup numbers on the READMEs (DiffEqGPU README: 'See GPUODEBenchmarks for comparison of our GPU solvers against CPUs and GPUs implementation in C++, JAX and PyTorch'). Ratios derived from page data (MPGOS ms / Julia ms), Tesla_V100 unadaptive: 2.118/0.2317 = 9.1x at n=8, 2.208/0.7853 = 2.8x at n=32768, but 94.157/145.317 = 0.65x at n=8,388,608; Tesla_V100 adaptive: 6.9x at n=8, 1.4x at n=131072, 0.70x at n=8,388,608. RTX_5000 unadaptive: 2.5x at n=8 up to 5.4x at n=2,097,152 and 4.8x at n=8,388,608 (886.082 vs 183.920 ms); RTX_5000 adaptive: 0.57x at n=8 (0.144 vs 0.253 ms), 1.08x at n=32768, 2.3x at n=8,388,608.
compiler_and_flags: MPGOS: nvcc -o Lorenz.exe -O3 -std=c++11 --ptxas-options=-v --gpu-architecture=sm_70 -lineinfo -maxrregcount=128 (GPU_ODE_MPGOS/makefile), BlockSize 1024, float precision. Julia: DiffEqGPU.vectorized_solve / vectorized_asolve with GPUTsit5(), CUDA.jl, BenchmarkTools minimum time (GPU_ODE_Julia/bench_lorenz_gpu.jl); Julia and CUDA.jl versions not stated in the files read.
hardware: NVIDIA Tesla V100 and RTX 5000 (from the data folder names Tesla_V100 and RTX_5000); host CPU model not stated
stars_or_usage: 329 stars (DiffEqGPU.jl); 27 stars (GPUODEBenchmarks); part of the DifferentialEquations.jl ecosystem
tradeoffs: Specialised to many small independent ODEs (one trajectory per GPU thread); not a solver for one large ODE. Needs CUDA.jl (the only backend that the JAX, PyTorch and MPGOS comparison supports). Julia startup and compile time are excluded from the timings.
caveats: Mixed result, not a uniform win: on the V100 Julia is slower than MPGOS for the largest ensembles (0.62x to 0.88x from n=131072 fixed-step and n=524288 adaptive) and on the RTX 5000 adaptive runs it is slower for n<=8192. The algorithms differ: Julia runs the Tsit5 tableau in both modes while MPGOS runs RK4 (fixed) and RKCK45 (adaptive), and MPGOS tolerances are not set in Lorenz.cu, so equal work is not shown. MPGOS is built with --gpu-architecture=sm_70 only, so the RTX 5000 (Turing, sm_75, if it is the Quadro RTX 5000; model not spelled out in the files read) probably ran JIT-compiled PTX; this may inflate the RTX 5000 ratios. The benchmark repo was last committed 2024-01-04, so the data predate current DiffEqGPU.jl versions. MPGOS times use clock() around Solve() plus synchronisation; Julia uses BenchmarkTools minimum over CUDA.@sync, so statistics differ. float32 only. The source states no mechanism for the gap at small n (the MPGOS rows are near 2 ms flat for n<=8192 on V100, which looks like a fixed launch/setup cost). The CMAME 2024 paper (Utkarsh et al., 'Automated translation and accelerated solving of differential equations on multiple GPU platforms') carries the headline claims but was not opened (journal and arXiv blocked), so no paper numbers are quoted. The repo README says the Julia solver lives in DiffEqGPU.jl and GPUODEBenchmarks only holds the scripts and data.
found_via: SciML/DiffEqGPU.jl README 'Benchmarks' section pointing at utkarsh530/GPUODEBenchmarks; data files paper_artifacts/data/{Tesla_V100,RTX_5000}/{CPP,Julia}/*_times_{adaptive,unadaptive}.txt fetched via raw.githubusercontent.com

name: Mojo (explicit SIMD) in mojo-analyze: Mandelbrot
baseline: Scalar C Mandelbrot in the same repo (c/mandelbrot.c, clang -O3 -ffp-contract=off, standard library only)
workload: Escape-time Mandelbrot over 800x600 pixels, max 500 iterations, Float64, checksum of per-pixel iteration counts verified equal across all variants; timing of the core computation only, 2 warmups and 7 measured trials, mean reported.
claimed_speedup: ANALYSIS.md Mandelbrot table: Mojo (SIMD) 0.0554 s, C (-O3, scalar) 0.0904 s (1.6x slower), Rust (scalar, release) 0.1114 s (2.0x slower). README: 'Mojo wins the SIMD-heavy Mandelbrot case ... 1.6x faster than C'. The same repo reports C ahead of Mojo on the other four categories (sieve 1.05x, word-frequency 1.6x, CSV aggregation 2.3x, JSON parsing 2.3x).
compiler_and_flags: Mojo 1.0.0: mojo build --fp-mode contract=off benchmarks/mandelbrot/mandelbrot.mojo; C: Apple clang 21, clang -O3 -ffp-contract=off -o dist/mandelbrot-c c/mandelbrot.c (pixi.toml build and build-c tasks); no -march=native, no LTO or PGO.
hardware: Apple M4 Pro, 14 cores, 24 GB RAM, macOS 26.5.2, arm64 (Linux x86_64 and arm64 CI runners are a secondary reference, no C row there yet)
tradeoffs: The Mojo kernel is hand-vectorised (SIMD[DType.float64, 4] with a per-lane active mask and a scalar remainder loop), so it costs more code than the C loop. Mojo needs --fp-mode contract=off here: the default fused-multiply-add contraction changed the checksum by 10 out of about 42.4 million; clang -O3 on this platform shows the same drift unless -ffp-contract=off.
caveats: The comparison is explicitly not same-technique: the repo says Mojo wins 'specifically because it uses SIMD and the C/Rust versions don't' (C and Rust are plain scalar loops that rely on whatever autovectorisation the compiler manages). It therefore measures vectorisation ergonomics, not codegen quality, and a hand-vectorised C or C++ version (intrinsics or compiler vector extensions) would likely close the gap; none is provided. Single machine (arm64, 128-bit NEON), apparently single-author repo with 0 stars, Mojo 1.0.0 toolchain pinned. Same repo shows C ahead on every non-SIMD category.
found_via: WebSearch (github.com): 'Mojo implementation README faster than C++ OR Rust OR numpy benchmark pure Mojo' led to iinoshirozheng/mojo-analyze; README, ANALYSIS.md and pixi.toml read
why_faster: Explicit 4-lane Float64 SIMD with per-lane escape masks in Mojo versus plain scalar loops in C and Rust that depend on autovectorisation (the source's own explanation).

name: Julia in JuliaLang/Microbenchmarks: userfunc_mandelbrot
claimed_speedup: benchmarks.csv (Julia v1.0.0 era data): userfunc_mandelbrot C 0.076702 ms, Julia 0.052706 ms (1.46x faster than C, ratio 0.69 of C time, derived from page data). On the other benchmarks Julia takes 0.98x to 2.19x of C time: pi_sum 1.01, matrix_multiply 0.98 (both languages call OpenBLAS), quicksort 1.00, print_to_file 1.09, fibonacci 1.33, matrix_statistics 1.63, parse_integers 2.19 (derived).
compiler_and_flags: C: gcc 7.3.1 -std=c99 -O$N with the best timing taken over -O0..-O3 (Makefile); Julia v1.0.0 default optimisation, compile time excluded.
tradeoffs: Julia is JIT compiled; the timings exclude compile time and Julia start-up. Only a micro benchmark of 546 grid points.
caveats: One benchmark of eight where Julia beats C, and the suite page says its own results 'are a bit dated' (Julia 1.0.0, gcc 7.3.1, 2018 hardware); current CI results sit on julialang.github.io (blocked here). The source gives no mechanism. Reading the benchmark code, the C version multiplies C99 double complex values (z*z+c) without -ffast-math or -fcx-limited-range, and gcc then lowers complex multiplication to a call that performs NaN/Inf recovery, while the Julia and Fortran versions use the plain four-multiplication formula (inference by the searcher, not stated by the source); so this is probably a complex-arithmetic semantics difference, not Julia producing faster code from the same source, and it caps the tier at C. The Rust (0.75 of C time) and Go (0.78) rows of the same benchmark also beat C and are not recorded here (outside this language filter).

name: Fortran (gfortran) in JuliaLang/Microbenchmarks: userfunc_mandelbrot
claimed_speedup: benchmarks.csv: userfunc_mandelbrot C 0.076702 ms, Fortran 0.053836 ms (1.42x faster than C, ratio 0.70 of C time, derived from page data). Fortran is slower than C on most other benchmarks of the suite: matrix_multiply 1.16, matrix_statistics 1.54, quicksort 1.19, parse_integers 6.88, print_to_file 5.97 (derived); iteration_pi_sum 1.00 and fibonacci 0.99.
compiler_and_flags: C and Fortran both built with gcc/gfortran 7.3.1 (Makefile: $(CC) -std=c99 -O$* and $(FC) $(FFLAGS) -O$*), best timing over -O0..-O3 on each side.
tradeoffs: gfortran source uses complex(dp) with z**2 and a hand-written abs2; Fortran I/O and string parsing rows are far slower than C in the same suite.
caveats: Same suite and same caveats as the Julia row: data are Julia v1.0.0 / gcc 7.3.1 era (2018), the source gives no mechanism, and the win is on one benchmark of eight (Fortran loses badly on parse_integers and print_to_file). Probable cause (inference, not stated by the source) is C99 complex multiplication semantics in the C baseline rather than Fortran code generation; a C version using real arithmetic or -fcx-limited-range would probably match. This caps the tier at C.

name: Fortran (Intel ifort) in floatingspeed lap3dkernel: direct 1/r kernel sum
baseline: Plain OpenMP C++ version of the same 1/r kernel direct summation in the same repo (c++SIMD/lap3dkernel.cpp without VCL), built with g++ 9 and icpc 2019
workload: Dense direct N-body sum of the 3D 1/r kernel from 10,000 sources to 10,000 targets in double precision, 12 OpenMP threads, throughput in Gpair/s.
claimed_speedup: No claim by the source. lap3dkernel/README results on an Intel Xeon Gold 6128 (12 OMP threads): C++ (GCC 9) + omp 4.1 Gpair/s, C++ (icpc 2019) + omp 4.1, Fortran (GCC 9) + omp 4.0, Fortran (ifort 2019) + omp 7.7 Gpair/s, i.e. ifort Fortran is 1.88x the plain C++ (derived from page data). Hand-SIMD C++ with the VCL library gets 6.1 (g++) and 4.0 (icpc), and with a custom double rsqrt 18.3 (g++) and 12.8 (icpc), which beat the Fortran. On the i7-7700HQ laptop gfortran 7 is 1.3 vs C++ 1.1 Gpair/s.
compiler_and_flags: run_all_tests.sh (commented Intel lines): icpc -fPIC -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -mkl -qopenmp -std=c++17 and ifort lap3dpottest.f90 -qopenmp -fPIC -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -mkl; GNU: g++ -fPIC -O3 -march=native -funroll-loops -fopenmp -std=c++17, gfortran -O3 -fopenmp -funroll-loops -march=native. The README does not state that these exact flags produced the 2019 numbers.
hardware: Intel Xeon Gold 6128 (2019 workstation, 3.4 GHz, AVX-512, 12 cores, 12 OMP threads)
stars_or_usage: 8 stars; main author Alex Barnett; copyright Simons Foundation, Inc.
tradeoffs: The ifort row needs the proprietary Intel Fortran compiler (2019 version); gfortran matches plain C++.
caveats: The source makes no Fortran-beats-C++ claim and says 'Clearly C++ w/ VCL beats others by 2x, and nearly 4x w/ custom rsqrt' on the laptop; the ratio is read off the table by the searcher. The gap is ifort versus g++ and icpc on naive code, so it is a compiler effect, not a language effect (gfortran 4.0 equals g++ 4.1), and hand-vectorised C++ is faster than the Fortran. The newer repo Fortran adds SoA and SIMD variants that reach 8.1 Gpair/s on a Ryzen 5700U, equal to C++ with VCL (8.1), and the README results are partly unfinished ('... (to finish)'). Flags not tied to the numbers, one machine for the ifort row, 2019 compilers. The source gives no mechanism.
